contact_edits.before: There's humour, though less than the show or its first-night audience might like to think. Anna D. Shapiros production seems to have coarsened on the road, and to be aimed at people who think it shockingly funny to hear mature actresses using four-letter words. Most of the cast give in at some time or other; even Shannon Cochran, who otherwise dispenses a fastidious brand of swaggering self-hatred as Barbara, goes for an easy laugh at the second-act curtain. (She gets it; the public appetite for bad acting seems inexhaustible.) There's one character I haven't mentioned: a Cheyenne housekeeper (DeLanna Studi) who spends the first scene giving comfort to Beverly, the last giving it to Violet, and in between proves a very good cook and a great defender of virtue. Even the toughest American plays can wind up sentimental, and the final curtain of this one finds Violet the hitherto-untouchable curled up in the lap of the Indian (her word, though the others try to persuade her it's "Native American"). Perhaps this is a metaphor for America. Or it could just be a gimmick. - August: Osage County runs until Nov. 15. Call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.comfor tickets and information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com
